detail:

PLTR

Trading disclosure
Palantir Wins Knox Federal Partnership, Gains 4% ©yangwenshuang from Getty Images Signature and Aflo Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Palantir shares rose 4% today after Knox Systems announced a partnership to bring commercial software into FedRAMP and IL5 federal environments.

The deal lets other companies' software reach the government through Palantir's federal accreditations, which makes Palantir more central to how agencies get new technology.

No financial terms were disclosed, and analysts already expect revenue to climb from $4.48 billion in 2025 to $8.22 billion in 2026.

The next test is the third-quarter report, which management guided to $2.16 billion to $2.164 billion of revenue.

Palantir Technologies (PLTR:NASDAQ) shares are up 4% today after Knox Systems announced a partnership, before Monday's open, to get commercial software into the government's most tightly secured clouds.

That wins back part of Friday's 7% drop, which pushed the stock into a correction. (Tech is having a good day, too: the QQQ QQQ:NASDAQ is up nearly 2%.)

What exactly happened

Knox, which is private, runs a managed federal cloud and says it can get software makers FedRAMP authorization in 90 days or less. It already hosts more than 100 AI and enterprise applications, for customers including Adobe (ADBE:NASDAQ), Sierra and Armis.

Palantir has already helped software companies deploy to federal agencies on its own accredited infrastructure, IL5 environments included. Put the two together, and a software maker gets one route from authorization to deployment.

As Knox CEO Irina Denisenko said in the press release: "Knox exists to get the best software in the world to the government faster, and to protect it once it's there."

Neither company disclosed financial terms.

Palantir becomes the on-ramp

Those accreditations are the hard part for any software maker selling to the Pentagon, and this deal puts Palantir's to work for other companies' products.

It also lands on top of a government business that's already flying. Palantir's U.S. government revenue rose 90% year over year to $809 million in Q2 2026, out of $1.94 billion in total revenue.

Analysts expect revenue to nearly double again this year, to $8.22 billion, and to reach $17.9 billion by 2028…

Palantir Technologies (PLTR): revenue, actual and consensus estimates, $ billions, fiscal 2023–2028 (TIKR)

With no terms disclosed, there's nothing in today's news for analysts to add to those estimates yet.

The multiple already came down

At Friday's close, Palantir traded at 98x forward earnings. That's a touch below its five-year average of 103x and far from the 270x it hit in October 2025…

Palantir Technologies (PLTR): forward (NTM) P/E, last 5 years (TIKR)

Today's move puts it right back at that average. That's still a rich price, so the next real test is the third quarter, which management guided to $2.16 billion to $2.164 billion of revenue.

NEW YORK, Oct. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Stock Preachers News Commentary - U.S. 10-year Treasury yields fell about 17 basis points last week while the Nasdaq 100 dropped 5.5%, the largest same-week decline in both since the April 2025 tariff turmoil, Bloomberg reported. The move caught investors who had positioned heavily for a deeper slump in bonds, after 10-year yields climbed over the prior seven months to their highest levels in more than two decades. Active Companies from around the markets with current developments this week include: iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (NASDAQ: TLT), iShares 7-10 Year Treasury Bond ETF (NASDAQ: IEF), ProShares UltraShort 20+ Year Treasury (NYSE Arca: TBT), Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ: QQQ), CoreWeave, Inc. (NASDAQ: CRWV).

Stock Preachers Logo

The trigger was a sell-off in AI-linked technology stocks. As shares fell, Treasuries showed early signs of acting like a safe haven again, a role they have failed to play for much of the past few years, partly because oil-driven sell-offs can push stocks and bonds lower together. Commodity trading advisers, the trend-following funds that had built bearish Treasury futures positions at what Bloomberg described as 'extremely short' levels, exited those bets last week, adding fuel to the rally.

Rate expectations had swung hard. Traders at one point priced about a 50% chance of a Federal Reserve rate hike in October, and still expect one increase by year-end and another in 2027, according to Bloomberg. At the same time, the AI build-out has leaned on bond markets: investment-grade companies, led by megacap technology, have sold about $1.7 trillion of bonds this year, up about 29% from a year earlier.

"To paraphrase Mark Twain, rumors of the death of US Treasuries are greatly exaggerated," James Athey, a portfolio manager at Marlborough Investment Management, told Bloomberg.

In other industry developments and happenings in the market this week include:

iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (NASDAQ: TLT)

The long end did the heavy lifting. The iShares fund, which tracks U.S. Treasuries with more than 20 years to maturity, rose 2.65% last week, from $77.98 at the October 9 close to $80.05 on October 16, according to Stock Analysis data. The fund holds about $47 billion in assets and charges a 0.15% expense ratio. Long-dated bonds move the most in price when yields change, which is why the long end led the rally.

XLP rose 5% for its best week since February, while XLY slipped 0.35%.

SPY fell 1.97% for its worst week since June, and QQQ dropped 5.5%, its worst in over a year.

Cracker Barrel, Signet Jewelers and VF Corp. led the gainers, while Kandi, Six Flags and Newsmax led the decliners.

Defensive consumer names caught a bid last week as investors rotated out of a sharply weaker broader market. Cracker Barrel Old Country Store (CBRL), Signet Jewelers (SIG) and VF Corp. (VFC) were the standouts. Kandi Technologies (KNDI), Six Flags Entertainment (FUN) and Newsmax (NMAX) were among the laggards.

During the week of Oct. 12 to Oct. 16, the Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLP) climbed 5%, its best weekly performance since February. The Consumer Discretionary Select Sector SPDR Fund (XLY) moved the other way, slipping 0.35%.

See what 10M+ investors are talking about. Get the Stocktwits Daily Rip for what retail is watching right now, free to your inbox

The split came as the broader market struggled. The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (SPY) fell 1.97%, its worst week since June. The tech-heavy Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) dropped 5.5%, its steepest weekly loss in more than a year.

Cracker Barrel, Signet, VF Corp. Among Leading Gainers

Cracker Barrel's stock gained 20% over the week, adding to its 171% surge this year. A leadership shake-up and the reversal of a widely criticized brand overhaul have driven the rally. A costly logo redesign alienated the company's core customers, and CEO Julie Felss Masino stepped down in August.

Industry veteran David Deno took over as CEO, and the company quickly scrapped the rebrand and returned to its classic heritage look. That decision helped trigger a short squeeze and restored investor confidence.

The operational numbers have also backed up the story. In its fiscal fourth quarter (Q4), Cracker Barrel posted adjusted earnings of $0.99 per share, far above Wall Street's $0.18 estimate, on revenue of $849.3 million. Cost discipline and pricing adjustments lifted average guest checks, and the company strengthened its balance sheet with a $77 million sale-leaseback and the sale of its Maple Street Biscuit Company subsidiary.

Signet Jewelers stock climbed 12.6% on deal news. According to a Bloomberg report, the retailer and luxury group Richemont are in advanced talks to join a consortium to buy diamond miner De Beers. The Global Diamond Consortium is led by former De Beers CEO Gareth Penny. It emerged in July as the preferred bidder and is negotiating with Botswana, which is looking to raise its stake to around 25%.
